Dear Akash,

You asked how I am, and typing "fine" felt wrong, so here is the real answer. Two weeks ago I skidded on gravel riding home at eleven at night. My shoulder is bruised and the headaches kept coming back after dark. I finally told Mum and Dad everything on Sunday, and Dad took me to the doctor, who checked me over. I'm going back for a follow-up next week.

I have made new rules and taped them next to my helmet shelf: strap the helmet on every single ride, stay under the limit even when friends pull ahead, and no riding after nine at night. I'll take the bus instead. It feels like giving up some freedom, but it also feels like the fall taught me something. Come over and I'll tell you the whole story.

Aparna

qa.q: Which rules did Aparna tape next to the helmet shelf?
qa.a: Strap the helmet on every ride, stay under the limit, and no riding after nine at night.

qa.a: Aparna's feelings are mixed: it feels like giving up some freedom, but Aparna also feels the fall taught something useful.

qa.q: What else could Aparna do to make the new habits last, and why?
qa.a: Aparna could ask Akash or a friend to check in on the rules and keep the follow-up visit, because support makes new habits easier to keep.

qa.q: How might Aparna's parents have felt on hearing everything on Sunday?
qa.a: They were probably worried and also relieved that Aparna finally told them, since it let Dad take Aparna to the doctor.

"Elizabeth, you asked in this podcast how the accident changed me. Well, I, Swati, used to ride my scooter home from the night shift at eleven, fast, sometimes with the helmet on the handlebar because it messed up my hair.
In March a dog ran out and I went down on the flyover. Just scrapes, I thought. But for two weeks I had headaches and kept dropping things. I told Mummy, and she made me see a doctor that same week. The doctor checked me properly and said to come back if anything got worse. I was lucky.
I also talked to Mummy and my brother a lot. I cried more than I expected.
Then I made rules and told them the rules, so they'd hold me to it. Helmet, always, strapped. No riding after ten; I take the office cab. And I stay at the speed limit on the flyover, every time.
It's boring. It's also why I'm here."

qa.q: What time did Swati use to ride home from the night shift?
How did Swati feel after the accident, and what shows it?
qa.a: Swati was more shaken than expected, crying a lot while talking to family and having headaches and dropping things for two weeks.

qa.q: What else could Swati do to keep the new rules?
qa.a: Swati could keep telling family about the rules and ask them to check in, since sharing them already helps hold them in place.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the changes Swati made?
qa.a: Mummy, who pushed for the doctor visit, would likely feel relieved and reassured by the helmet, the cab and the slower riding.

grounding: Shows a shaken person talking with family, seeing a doctor for lingering symptoms and adopting stricter rules on helmets, speed and night riding.

I'm Anjali, and I live on the same floor as Eshaan in the hostel. He came back from the hospital on a Sunday in April with a bandaged hand and a quiet face. His bike had skidded on gravel at night on the highway.
For a week he barely came out of his room. Then I saw his parents visit, and I heard them talking with the door open for a long time. After that he went back to the doctor twice because the dizziness hadn't gone away.
The changes I noticed came slowly. His old helmet, the one with the broken strap, went into the bin. He bought a new one and wore it even to the shop across the road. He stopped taking the highway after dark and caught the college bus instead. When friends raced on the ring road, he said no.
I don't know exactly what he was feeling, but he seemed steadier by May.

qa.q: What happened to Eshaan's old helmet?
What might Eshaan have been feeling during the first week back?
qa.a: He was likely shaken and withdrawn, barely leaving his room after the skid.

qa.q: What else could Eshaan do if the memory of the accident keeps bothering him?
qa.a: He could talk to the college counsellor, since support can help with more than the physical injury.

qa.q: How do Eshaan's changes look to Anjali?
qa.a: Anjali notices the new helmet, the bus and his refusal to race, and thinks he seems steadier, though Anjali can't know exactly what he feels.

grounding: Shows a person shaken by an accident talking with family, seeing a doctor for lingering symptoms and changing habits on helmets, speed and night riding.
